excerpt: When an assault at work is covered by workers' compensation in Georgia and South Carolina, and the connection to employment that decides it.
keyTakeaways: Workplace violence injuries are covered by workers' comp when the violence is connected to employment — customer attacks, criminal acts during work, coworker disputes over work matters, and violence against high-risk workers all qualify. The aggressor is barred. Domestic violence at work is generally not covered. Beyond workers' comp, victims can file personal injury lawsuits against attackers and negligent security claims. Report within 30 days in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) or 90 days in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-20).

faqs.question: Are injuries from workplace violence covered by workers' comp?
faqs.answer: Yes — if the violence was connected to your employment. Workers' compensation covers injuries that arise out of and in the course of employment. Violence motivated by work disputes, criminal acts during work duties, and attacks on workers in high-risk occupations typically qualify. Violence from purely personal disputes may not.

faqs.question: What if I was the aggressor in a workplace fight?
faqs.answer: If you initiated the physical confrontation, your workers' comp claim will likely be denied in both Georgia and South Carolina. The aggressor defense bars coverage because the injury arose from your own voluntary conduct, not from employment. However, if a work-related argument escalated and you participated but did not start the physical altercation, coverage may still apply.

faqs.question: Is domestic violence at the workplace covered by workers' comp?
faqs.answer: Generally no — because the violence stems from a personal relationship, not employment. However, some courts have found coverage when the employer knew about a specific domestic violence threat and failed to take protective measures, or when the employment placed the worker at the location where the attack occurred.

faqs.question: Can I sue the person who attacked me at work in addition to filing a workers' comp claim?
faqs.answer: Yes. A workers' comp claim covers your medical bills and lost wages from your employer's insurer. A separate personal injury lawsuit against the attacker can recover pain and suffering, emotional distress, and punitive damages — compensation not available through workers' comp. You may also have a negligent security claim against the property owner.

faqs.question: How do I report a workplace violence injury in Georgia vs. South Carolina?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, report to your employer within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and file your claim within 1 year (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). In South Carolina, report within 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20) and file within 2 years (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Also file a police report to create an official record of the criminal act.

faqs.question: Does workers' comp cover PTSD from workplace violence?
faqs.answer: Both states provide limited coverage for psychological injuries from workplace violence, though the standards are more restrictive than for physical injuries. If the PTSD resulted from a traumatic workplace event — such as an assault, robbery, or active shooter incident — it may be covered. An attorney can evaluate whether your psychological injuries qualify.
